forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

findings.headline: The Fund had 3% of its assets invested in local levelling up assets at 31 March 2026, against an ambition of up to 5%.
findings.detail: The paper reports the Fund's local levelling up assets, led by M&G UK Residential Property at £46.8m, and says the government ambition was for funds to invest up to 5% of their assets in these projects. Emerging guidance places greater emphasis on local investment.
findings.matters: Other funds face the same local investment target and reporting requirements, so the 3% against 5% position is a benchmark for their own local investment plans.
findings.figures: 3% of assets in local levelling up investments at 31 March 2026; ambition up to 5%; M&G UK Residential Property £46.8m.
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the Fund has 3% invested in local levelling up assets.

findings.headline: 2,034 undecided leaver cases were processed in 2025/26, against a backlog of approximately 6,500 unprocessed leaver records at the end of 2024/25.
findings.detail: The paper says the Fund intends to reduce the backlog to below a sustainable baseline of 1,000 cases within three years, and that the project will continue into 2026/27. At 31 March 2026 the deferred membership count includes 6,868 open cases that may change status.
findings.matters: Backlogs of undecided leavers affect the accuracy of liability data that actuaries use at valuation, so other funds facing the same backlog can compare progress.
findings.figures: Backlog approximately 6,500 records at end 2024/25; 2,034 cases processed in 2025/26; target below 1,000 cases within 3 years; 6,868 open undecided-leaver cases at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Total management expenses were £20.451m in 2025-26 against a £17.930m budget, with non-invoiced investment management expenses at £14.415m against £12.400m.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the non-invoiced investment fees to global equities outperforming the discount rate, which raised asset values and associated fees, together with additional commitments to alternative funds. It attributes higher oversight and governance costs (£1.589m against a £1.247m budget) to unplanned spending arising from the Government's Fit for the Future agenda after the rejection of ACCESS's proposal.
findings.matters: Fees linked to asset values and to pooling transition costs are a growing cost line for LGPS funds, and other finance teams can compare how their budgets absorb similar pressures.
findings.figures: Total management expenses £20.451m actual vs £17.930m budget; non-invoiced investment management expenses £14.415m vs £12.400m; oversight and governance costs £1.589m vs £1.247m; administrative costs £3.421m vs £3.369m.
findings.quote: Investment management expenses (non - invoiced) are higher than budget

findings.headline: Contributions of £161.261m against a £153.000m budget in 2025-26, which the paper attributes to salary increases above the actuarial assumption.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast variance on contributions is due to actual salary increases being much higher than the assumption used from the 2022 valuation. Contributions from employers are set at the rate recommended by the actuary.
findings.matters: Pay awards running above actuarial assumptions raise contribution income, but also raise the liability measured at the next valuation, which finance directors weigh together.
findings.figures: Contributions £161.261m actual against £153.000m budget; benefits payable £137.625m against £136.000m budget.
findings.quote: is due to actual salary increases being much higher than the actuarial salary increase assumption used from the 2022 valuation

findings.headline: Employers paid £558k of the £161.261m contributions received in 2025-26 late.
findings.detail: The paper reports that 99.65% of contributions were paid on time. It says the Fund did not apply any charges or levies for late payment and made no reports to The Pensions Regulator. The text gives the late share as 0.3%, while the table gives 0.35%.
findings.matters: Late employer payments affect cash flow and reporting, and a finance officer at another council can compare late-payment levels and enforcement decisions.
findings.figures: £558k paid late of £161.261m total contributions; 0.35% paid late in the table; 0.3% stated in the text; employer late payments £418k; employee late payments £140k.
findings.quote: of the total amount of contributions received, only 0.3% (£558k) was paid late by employers.
